paragraphs.text: When an ocean cable breaks, who fixes it?

Most people never see it. Cable ships are limited to a speed of eight knots while laying cable so it lies properly on the sea floor. A cable's position must be carefully mapped as it is laid. In 1866 the SS Great Eastern successfully laid two transatlantic cables. Oersted, built in 1872 for the Great Northern Telegraph Company, was the first ship specifically designed for cable repair. USNS Zeus can lay about 1,600 km of cable to a depth of 2,700 m. Cable engines can feed 240 m of cable a minute. Goliath was the first ship to lay an ocean cable, in 1850. Every new or broken submarine cable depends on a cable ship to lay or repair it.
Here is how it works. A cable ship pays out cable at low speed along a carefully mapped route, and in repairs grapples the cable from the seabed and splices it on deck.
That is the bottleneck. Cable ships are purpose-built, carry specialised handling gear and trained crews, and cannot be improvised from ordinary vessels.
The failure would not stay contained. When repair ships are busy or far away, a damaged cable stays down longer and traffic runs on thinner backup routes.
So what protects the system? Regional maintenance agreements keep repair ships on standby, and route diversity keeps traffic moving while a repair waits.
